body.en:
An operator is a symbol or keyword that performs an operation on values (operands) in an SQL expression or condition.

1. Arithmetic operators

+ addition, - subtraction, * multiplication, / division. They are used in SELECT expressions and in conditions. Oracle has no % operator; use MOD(). Any arithmetic with NULL gives NULL.

2. Comparison (relational) operators

OperatorMeaning
=equal to
<>, !=, ^=not equal to
>, <greater than, less than
>=, <=greater/less than or equal to

3. Logical operators

  • AND: true if both conditions are true.
  • OR: true if at least one condition is true.
  • NOT: reverses the result of a condition.

Operator precedence (highest first)

  1. Brackets ( )
  2. * /
  3. + - and || (concatenation)
  4. Comparison operators, IN, LIKE, BETWEEN, IS NULL
  5. NOT
  6. AND
  7. OR

Because AND is evaluated before OR, use brackets when mixing them:

SELECT ename, sal * 12 AS annual
FROM emp
WHERE sal * 12 > 500000
AND (job = 'MANAGER' OR job = 'ANALYST');

h.en: Special Operators: IN, BETWEEN and IS NULL

body.en:
WHERE col IN (v1, v2, ...)
WHERE col BETWEEN low AND high
WHERE col LIKE 'pattern'
WHERE col IS NULL
WHERE col > ANY (sub-query)
WHERE col > ALL (sub-query)
WHERE EXISTS (sub-query)
  • IN (list): true if the value matches any value in the list. It replaces many OR conditions. NOT IN is the opposite (be careful: if the list contains NULL, NOT IN returns no rows).
  • BETWEEN low AND high: true if the value is in the range, including both limits. NOT BETWEEN gives values outside the range. It works for numbers, dates and text.
  • IS NULL / IS NOT NULL: test for missing values. = NULL never works because NULL is not equal to anything, not even another NULL.

LIKE compares a text value with a pattern containing wildcard characters:

  • % (percent) matches zero or more characters.
  • _ (underscore) matches exactly one character.

Examples: 'S%' starts with S; '%AN' ends with AN; '%RA%' contains RA; '__J%' 3rd letter J; '_____' exactly 5 characters.

  • LIKE is case-sensitive in Oracle; use UPPER(col) LIKE 'S%' for a case-insensitive search.
  • To search for a real % or _, define an escape character: WHERE code LIKE 'A\_%' ESCAPE '\'.
  • NOT LIKE returns rows that do not match the pattern.

h.en: Special Operators: ANY, ALL and EXISTS

body.en:
These operators are used with a sub-query (or a list) that returns several values.

  • ANY (SOME): the condition is true if it holds for at least one value returned.
  • ALL: the condition is true only if it holds for every value returned.
  • EXISTS: true if the sub-query returns at least one row; NOT EXISTS is true if it returns no rows.
ConditionEquivalent
> ANY (list)greater than the minimum
< ANY (list)less than the maximum
= ANY (list)same as IN
> ALL (list)greater than the maximum
< ALL (list)less than the minimum
<> ALL (list)same as NOT IN

EXISTS is usually used with a correlated sub-query and stops at the first matching row, so it is efficient.

title.en: 2.2 DUAL Table, Numeric and Character Functions

h.en: SQL Functions and the DUAL Table

body.en:
A function is a built-in program that takes arguments, performs an operation and returns a value. Functions are used in SELECT lists, WHERE, ORDER BY and other clauses.

Types of functions

  1. Single-row (scalar) functions: work on each row separately and return one result per row.
    • Character, numeric, date, conversion and general (NVL, DECODE) functions.
  2. Multiple-row (group / aggregate) functions: work on a group of rows and return one result per group: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN.

The DUAL table

DUAL is a dummy table automatically created by Oracle in the SYS schema and accessible to all users. It has one column (DUMMY, VARCHAR2(1)) and one row (value 'X').

Since SELECT always needs a FROM clause in Oracle, DUAL is used to evaluate expressions, test functions or get values like SYSDATE that do not come from a table. Because it has one row, the result is shown once.

SQL> SELECT 25 * 4 + 10 FROM dual;

25*4+10
-------
    110

FunctionPurposeExample → Result
ABS(n)absolute (positive) valueABS(-25) → 25
POWER(m, n)m raised to the power nPOWER(2, 5) → 32
MOD(m, n)remainder of m / nMOD(17, 5) → 2
SQRT(n)square root (n ≥ 0)SQRT(144) → 12
ROUND(n, d)rounds to d decimal placesROUND(156.786, 2) → 156.79
ROUND(n, -d)rounds left of the decimal pointROUND(156.786, -1) → 160
TRUNC(n, d)cuts to d decimals (no rounding)TRUNC(156.786, 2) → 156.78
CEIL(n)smallest integer ≥ nCEIL(12.1) → 13
FLOOR(n)largest integer ≤ nFLOOR(12.9) → 12
SIGN(n)-1, 0 or 1SIGN(-8) → -1
  • If d is omitted in ROUND/TRUNC, it is 0 (whole number).
  • ROUND vs TRUNC: ROUND(15.67) = 16 but TRUNC(15.67) = 15.
  • CEIL vs FLOOR: CEIL(-4.2) = -4 and FLOOR(-4.2) = -5.
  • MOD(m, 0) returns m.

FunctionPurposeExample → Result
LOWER(s)all small lettersLOWER('GTU') → gtu
UPPER(s)all capital lettersUPPER('gtu') → GTU
INITCAP(s)first letter of each word capitalINITCAP('surat city') → Surat City
LENGTH(s)number of charactersLENGTH('Gujarat') → 7
CONCAT(a, b)joins two stringsCONCAT('Diploma', 'One') → DiplomaOne
LTRIM(s, set)removes chars from the leftLTRIM('xxGTU', 'x') → GTU
RTRIM(s, set)removes chars from the rightRTRIM('GTUxx', 'x') → GTU
TRIM(s)removes spaces from both endsTRIM(' GTU ') → GTU
REPLACE(s, a, b)replaces every a by bREPLACE('JACK', 'J', 'BL') → BLACK
SUBSTR(s, m, n)n chars from position mSUBSTR('GUJARAT', 3, 3) → JAR
INSTR(s, t, m, n)position of n-th t from mINSTR('GUJARAT', 'A', 1, 2) → 6
LPAD(s, n, c)pads on the left to length nLPAD('77', 5, '*') → ***77
RPAD(s, n, c)pads on the right to length nRPAD('77', 5, '*') → 77***
  • LTRIM and RTRIM remove spaces when the second argument is omitted. They remove any character from the set, not the exact string: LTRIM('abcabcX', 'abc') → X.
  • SUBSTR positions start at 1; a negative start counts from the end. Without n it returns up to the end.
  • INSTR returns 0 when the text is not found. m and n are optional (default 1).
  • The || operator also concatenates and can join more than two strings: ename || ' (' || job || ')'.

Oracle stores a DATE as century, year, month, day, hour, minute and second. The default display format is DD-MON-YY. SYSDATE returns the current date and time of the database server.

FunctionPurposeExample → Result
SYSDATEcurrent date and timeSYSDATE → 28-OCT-26
ADD_MONTHS(d, n)adds n months (n can be −)ADD_MONTHS('28-OCT-26', 3) → 28-JAN-27
MONTHS_BETWEEN(d1, d2)months from d2 to d1MONTHS_BETWEEN('28-DEC-26', '28-OCT-26') → 2
LAST_DAY(d)last date of the monthLAST_DAY('28-OCT-26') → 31-OCT-26
NEXT_DAY(d, 'day')next given weekday after dNEXT_DAY('28-OCT-26', 'MONDAY') → 02-NOV-26
ROUND(d, 'MONTH')nearest 1st of monthROUND('28-OCT-26', 'MONTH') → 01-NOV-26
TRUNC(d, 'MONTH')1st of the same monthTRUNC('28-OCT-26', 'MONTH') → 01-OCT-26
ROUND(d, 'YEAR')nearest 1st JanuaryROUND('28-OCT-26', 'YEAR') → 01-JAN-27
TRUNC(d, 'YEAR')1st January of the yearTRUNC('28-OCT-26', 'YEAR') → 01-JAN-26

Rules

  • ROUND with 'MONTH' rounds up from the 16th day; with 'YEAR' from 1st July. ROUND/TRUNC without a format work on the day (remove the time).
  • ADD_MONTHS on the last day of a month gives the last day of the result month.
  • MONTHS_BETWEEN can return a fraction; it is negative if d1 is earlier than d2.

Date arithmetic

ExpressionResult
date + ndate n days later
date − ndate n days earlier
date − datenumber of days between
date + n/24adds n hours

Two dates cannot be added.

Conversion functions change a value from one data type to another. Oracle also converts types automatically (implicit conversion), but explicit conversion with these functions is clearer and safer.

  • TO_CHAR(date, 'fmt'): date → text in the given format.
  • TO_CHAR(number, 'fmt'): number → formatted text.
  • TO_DATE(text, 'fmt'): text → DATE. The format describes how the text is written.
  • TO_NUMBER(text, 'fmt'): text → NUMBER.

Date format elements

ElementMeaningFor 28-OCT-2026
DDday of month28
DY / DAYshort / full weekdayWED / WEDNESDAY
MMmonth number10
MON / MONTHshort / full month nameOCT / OCTOBER
YY / YYYY2- / 4-digit year26 / 2026
HH24:MI:SShours (0–23), minutes, seconds10:30:15
Qquarter4
fmremoves padding spacesOctober (not 'October ')

Number format elements

ElementMeaningExample
9a digitTO_CHAR(123, '9999') → ' 123'
0leading zeroTO_CHAR(45, '0000') → ' 0045'
, .thousands separator, decimal pointTO_CHAR(1234.5, '9,999.99') → ' 1,234.50'
$dollar signTO_CHAR(500, '$999') → ' $500'

If the number does not fit the format, Oracle shows ####.

h.en: General Functions: NVL, NVL2, DECODE and CASE

body.en:
• NVL(expr1, expr2): returns expr2 if expr1 is NULL, otherwise expr1. Both must have the same type. NVL(comm, 0).
  • NVL2(expr1, expr2, expr3): returns expr2 if expr1 is NOT NULL, otherwise expr3.
  • NULLIF(a, b): returns NULL if a = b, otherwise a.
  • DECODE(expr, search1, result1, search2, result2, ..., default): Oracle's IF-THEN-ELSE. It compares expr with each search value in order and returns the matching result; if nothing matches it returns the default (or NULL).
  • CASE: the ANSI standard conditional expression; it can test ranges and any conditions, whereas DECODE only tests equality.
SELECT ename, sal,
  CASE
    WHEN sal >= 50000 THEN 'HIGH'
    WHEN sal >= 25000 THEN 'MEDIUM'
    ELSE 'LOW'
  END AS category
FROM emp
WHERE deptno = 30;
ENAME   SAL CATEGORY
----- ----- --------
PRIYA 58000 HIGH
SUNIL 30000 MEDIUM
POOJA 28000 MEDIUM
VIJAY 20000 LOW

GREATEST(list) and LEAST(list) return the largest and smallest values of a list.

title.en: 2.4 Aggregate Functions, GROUP BY, HAVING and ORDER BY

body.en:
Aggregate functions work on a set of rows and return a single value. They can be used on the whole table or on groups made by GROUP BY.

FunctionReturns
COUNT(*)number of rows (including NULLs and duplicates)
COUNT(col)number of non-NULL values in col
COUNT(DISTINCT col)number of different non-NULL values
SUM(col)total of the values (numbers only)
AVG(col)average of the values (numbers only)
MAX(col)largest value (number, text or date)
MIN(col)smallest value (number, text or date)
  • All aggregate functions ignore NULL values, except COUNT(*). So AVG(comm) = SUM of the commissions ÷ number of non-NULL commissions. Use AVG(NVL(comm, 0)) to count NULLs as 0.
  • DISTINCT or ALL (the default) can be used inside: SUM(DISTINCT sal).
  • An aggregate cannot be used in WHERE; use HAVING.
  • Without GROUP BY, a SELECT with an aggregate cannot also list a normal column (ORA-00937: not a single-group group function).

SELECT col, aggregate(col2)
FROM table
[WHERE row_condition]
GROUP BY col
[HAVING group_condition]
[ORDER BY col [ASC | DESC]];

GROUP BY divides the rows of a table into groups that have the same value in the given column(s). The aggregate functions are then calculated for each group, and the query returns one row per group.

  • Every column in SELECT that is not inside an aggregate function must be written in GROUP BY. (A GROUP BY column need not appear in SELECT.)
  • Grouping can be on several columns: GROUP BY deptno, job makes one group for every combination.
  • NULL values form a group of their own.
  • Column aliases cannot be used in GROUP BY.

HAVING applies a condition to the groups, after grouping. It is normally used with aggregate functions: HAVING COUNT(*) > 2.

WHERE vs HAVING

WHEREHAVING
Filters individual rowsFilters groups
Applied before GROUP BYApplied after GROUP BY
Cannot use aggregate functionsUsually uses aggregate functions
Can be used without GROUP BYNormally used with GROUP BY
Used in SELECT, UPDATE, DELETEUsed only in SELECT

h.en: ORDER BY Clause and Order of Execution

body.en:
ORDER BY sorts the rows of the result. It is always the last clause of a SELECT.

ORDER BY col1 [ASC | DESC]
        [NULLS FIRST | NULLS LAST],
         col2 [ASC | DESC], ...
  • ASC (ascending) is the default; DESC gives descending order.
  • Several columns: rows are sorted by the first column, and rows with equal values are sorted by the next one.
  • You can sort by a column name, an expression, a column alias or a column position (ORDER BY 2). The column need not be in the SELECT list (except with DISTINCT).
  • NULLs are treated as the largest values: last in ASC, first in DESC (unless NULLS FIRST/LAST is given).
  • Numbers sort by value, dates from earliest to latest, and text alphabetically (capital letters before small letters).
  • Without ORDER BY, the order of rows is not guaranteed.

Logical order of execution

FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY. That is why an alias defined in SELECT can be used in ORDER BY but not in WHERE or HAVING.

h.en: Joins: Inner (Equi), Natural and Non-Equi Join

body.en:
A join combines rows from two or more tables based on a related column, so that data stored in separate tables (normalised data) can be shown together.

Types of joins: inner join (equi, natural, non-equi), outer join (left, right, full), cross join and self join.

Inner join

Returns only those rows that have matching values in both tables. Unmatched rows of either table are left out.

SELECT t1.col, t2.col
FROM t1 [INNER] JOIN t2
ON t1.key = t2.key;

-- Oracle traditional syntax
SELECT t1.col, t2.col
FROM t1, t2
WHERE t1.key = t2.key;
  • Equi join: the join condition uses the equality operator =, usually primary key = foreign key.
  • When the same column name exists in both tables, it must be qualified with the table name or alias (e.deptno), otherwise ORA-00918: column ambiguously defined.
  • To join n tables you need at least n − 1 join conditions.

Natural join and USING

SELECT ename, dname
FROM emp NATURAL JOIN dept;

SELECT ename, dname
FROM emp JOIN dept USING (deptno);

A natural join automatically joins on all columns with the same name in both tables (and shows the common column once). USING (col) names the common column explicitly.

Non-equi join

A join whose condition uses an operator other than =, such as BETWEEN, <, >. Example: finding each employee's salary grade from the SALGRADE table using e.sal BETWEEN s.losal AND s.hisal.

h.en: Outer Joins: Left, Right and Full

body.en:
An outer join returns the matching rows plus the rows that have no match in the other table. The missing columns are filled with NULL.

FROM t1 LEFT  [OUTER] JOIN t2 ON ...
FROM t1 RIGHT [OUTER] JOIN t2 ON ...
FROM t1 FULL  [OUTER] JOIN t2 ON ...

-- Oracle (+) syntax: + on the side
-- that may have no matching row
WHERE e.deptno = d.deptno(+)  -- LEFT
WHERE e.deptno(+) = d.deptno  -- RIGHT
  • LEFT OUTER JOIN: all rows from the left table + matching rows of the right table. Example: every employee, even one without a department.
  • RIGHT OUTER JOIN: all rows from the right table + matching rows of the left table. Example: every department, even one without employees.
  • FULL OUTER JOIN: all rows from both tables, matched where possible.
  • The Oracle (+) operator is placed on the side of the deficient table (the one whose columns may be NULL). It cannot be used for a full outer join.

Inner join vs outer join

Inner joinOuter join
Only matching rowsMatching + non-matching rows
No NULLs addedNULLs for missing columns
One typeLeft, right, full
Fewer (or equal) rowsMore (or equal) rows

A cross join returns the Cartesian product of two tables: every row of the first table combined with every row of the second. If the tables have m and n rows, the result has m × n rows.

SELECT c.color, s.sz
FROM colors c CROSS JOIN sizes s;

SELECT c.color, s.sz
FROM colors c, sizes s;
  • It has no join condition.
  • A cross join happens accidentally when the join condition is forgotten in the traditional syntax; with large tables this produces a huge result.
  • Uses: generating all combinations (colours × sizes, students × subjects), test data.

A self join joins a table with itself. The same table is used twice with two different aliases, as if they were two separate tables.

SELECT w.ename worker, m.ename manager
FROM emp w JOIN emp m
ON w.mgr = m.empno;
  • Used when a table has a column that refers to another row of the same table (a recursive relationship), e.g. emp.mgr refers to emp.empno of the manager.
  • Other uses: finding employees in the same city, students with the same marks, or comparing rows within a table.
  • A self join can be an inner join or an outer join (LEFT JOIN keeps the employee who has no manager).

A sub-query (inner query / nested query) is a SELECT statement written inside another SQL statement (the outer query). The result of the inner query is used by the outer query.

SELECT columns FROM table
WHERE col operator
      (SELECT col FROM table
       WHERE condition);

Rules

  • A sub-query is enclosed in brackets and is usually placed on the right side of the comparison.
  • A simple (non-correlated) sub-query runs once, before the outer query.
  • ORDER BY is not allowed inside a sub-query in WHERE.
  • Use single-row operators with single-row sub-queries and multiple-row operators with multiple-row sub-queries.

Types

  1. Single-row sub-query: returns exactly one value; used with = <> > < >= <=. Often uses an aggregate (MAX, AVG).
  2. Multiple-row sub-query: returns several rows; used with IN, NOT IN, ANY, ALL, EXISTS. If = is used with many rows, ORA-01427 occurs.
  3. Multiple-column sub-query: returns more than one column: WHERE (deptno, sal) IN (SELECT deptno, MAX(sal) ... GROUP BY deptno).
  4. Nested sub-query: a sub-query inside another sub-query. The innermost one runs first.
  5. Correlated sub-query: uses columns of the outer query (next topic).

Sub-queries can also be used in INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, CREATE TABLE and in the FROM clause (an inline view):

-- in UPDATE
UPDATE emp SET sal = sal * 1.1
WHERE deptno = (SELECT deptno FROM dept
                WHERE dname = 'SALES');

-- in FROM (inline view)
SELECT d, avg_sal
FROM (SELECT deptno d, AVG(sal) avg_sal
      FROM emp GROUP BY deptno)
WHERE avg_sal > 40000;

A correlated sub-query is a sub-query that refers to a column of the outer query. Because it depends on the current outer row, it is executed once for each row processed by the outer query.

Working

  1. The outer query takes a candidate row.
  2. The inner query is executed using the values of that row.
  3. The outer row is kept or rejected depending on the inner result.
  4. The steps repeat for the next outer row.

Nested vs correlated sub-query

Nested (simple)Correlated
Inner query is independentInner query uses outer columns
Executed onceExecuted once per outer row
Inner runs first, then outerOuter row first, then inner
FasterSlower for big tables
Can run aloneCannot run alone

Typical uses: comparing each row with its own group (salary above the department average), EXISTS / NOT EXISTS tests, finding the top earner in each department.

h.en: Set Operators: UNION, UNION ALL, INTERSECT and MINUS

body.en:
Set operators combine the results of two or more SELECT statements into one result.

SELECT col_list FROM t1
UNION | UNION ALL | INTERSECT | MINUS
SELECT col_list FROM t2
[ORDER BY ...];
OperatorReturns
UNIONall distinct rows from both queries (duplicates removed, sorted)
UNION ALLall rows from both queries, including duplicates (not sorted, fastest)
INTERSECTonly the rows common to both queries
MINUSrows of the first query that are not in the second

Rules

  • Each SELECT must have the same number of columns, and the corresponding columns must have compatible data types.
  • The column headings are taken from the first SELECT.
  • ORDER BY may appear only once, at the end, and applies to the whole result.
  • All set operators have equal precedence and are evaluated from top to bottom; use brackets to change the order.
  • UNION and INTERSECT are commutative (order of queries does not matter); MINUS is not.

Join vs set operator

A join combines columns of tables side by side (horizontally); a set operator combines rows of query results (vertically).

expl.en:
All Unit 2 queries use these three tables (the classic Oracle SCOTT schema with Indian names).

  • DEPT: 4 departments. Department 40 (OPERATIONS) has no employees, which is useful for outer joins.
  • EMP: 10 employees. mgr holds the empno of the employee's manager (used in the self join). Only salesmen have a comm (commission); others have NULL. MEHUL (110) is a trainee with no department (deptno NULL).
  • SALGRADE: salary ranges for grades 1–5 (used in the non-equi join).

SYSDATE is taken as 28-OCT-26 in all outputs.

code.en:
SELECT ename, sal,
       sal * 12 annual,
       sal + 1000 * 2 a,
       (sal + 1000) * 2 b,
       sal + comm total
FROM emp
WHERE deptno = 30;

expl.en:
• Arithmetic operators: + - * /. They work on NUMBER (and DATE) values.
  • Precedence: * and / are done before + and -. So sal + 1000 * 2 = sal + 2000, while (sal + 1000) * 2 adds first. Brackets change the order.
  • Any arithmetic with NULL gives NULL. PRIYA and VIJAY have no commission, so their total is blank. Use NVL(comm, 0) to fix this (see the NVL program).

programs.out:

----- -------
NEHA  ANALYST
KIRAN CLERK
VIJAY CLERK

ENAME DEPTNO
----- ------
PRIYA     30
SUNIL     30
POOJA     30
VIJAY     30

ENAME   SAL
----- -----
NEHA  45000
SUNIL 30000
HETAL 40000

expl.en:
• IN (list) is true if the value equals any value in the list. It is a short form of job = 'CLERK' OR job = 'ANALYST'.
  • NOT IN is the opposite. MEHUL (deptno NULL) is not returned: a comparison with NULL is never true.
  • BETWEEN a AND b includes both limits: sal >= 30000 AND sal <= 50000. The smaller value must come first. It also works with dates and text.

expl.en:
• % = any number of characters (even zero); _ = exactly one character.
  • 'P%': starts with P. '%A': ends with A. '_I%': second letter is I.
  • '____' (4 underscores): names with exactly 4 letters.
  • NOT LIKE '%A%': names that contain no A at all.
  • LIKE is case-sensitive. To search for a real % or _, use ESCAPE: LIKE '%\_%' ESCAPE '\'.

title.en: IS NULL and IS NOT NULL

programs.out:
ENAME COMM
----- ----
SUNIL 3000
POOJA 5000

ENAME  JOB
------ ---------
RAJESH PRESIDENT

no rows selected

expl.en:
• NULL means unknown, so it cannot be compared with =. Use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL.
  • RAJESH is the president and has no manager, so mgr IS NULL finds him.
  • comm = NULL is never true (the result is "unknown"), so it returns no rows even though 8 employees have no commission. This is a common mistake.

title.en: ANY and ALL with a sub-query

programs.out:
ENAME    SAL
------ -----
RAJESH 90000
AMIT   60000

ENAME   SAL
----- -----
VIJAY 20000
MEHUL 15000

expl.en:
• > ALL: greater than every value in the list, i.e. greater than the maximum. The highest salary in dept 30 is 58000, so only 90000 and 60000 qualify.
  • < ANY: less than at least one value, i.e. less than the maximum. The clerks earn 22000 and 20000, so salaries below 22000 qualify.
  • Summary: > ANY = more than the minimum; < ALL = less than the minimum; = ANY is the same as IN.

code.en:
SELECT d.deptno, d.dname
FROM dept d
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM emp e
              WHERE e.deptno = d.deptno);

SELECT d.deptno, d.dname
FROM dept d
WHERE NOT EXISTS
      (SELECT 1 FROM emp e
       WHERE e.deptno = d.deptno);

programs.out:
DEPTNO DNAME
------ --------
    10 ACCOUNTS
    20 RESEARCH
    30 SALES

DEPTNO DNAME
------ ----------
    40 OPERATIONS

expl.en:
• EXISTS is true if the sub-query returns at least one row. The values returned do not matter, so SELECT 1 is common.
  • For each department, the inner query checks whether some employee works there (a correlated sub-query).
  • NOT EXISTS finds departments with no employees: OPERATIONS (40).
  • EXISTS stops searching at the first match, so it is often faster than IN for large tables.

code.en:
SELECT ABS(-25) a, POWER(2, 5) p,
       MOD(17, 5) m, SQRT(144) s
FROM dual;

SELECT ROUND(156.786, 2) r1,
       ROUND(156.786) r2,
       ROUND(156.786, -1) r3,
       TRUNC(156.786, 2) t1,
       TRUNC(156.786) t2
FROM dual;

SELECT CEIL(12.1) c, FLOOR(12.9) f,
       ROUND(-2.5) r, TRUNC(-2.7) t
FROM dual;

expl.en:
DUAL is a special one-row, one-column table owned by SYS. It is used to calculate expressions or call functions that do not need any table.

  • ABS(n): absolute value. POWER(m, n): mn. MOD(m, n): remainder of m ÷ n. SQRT(n): square root.
  • ROUND(n, d): rounds to d decimal places (5 and above goes up). A negative d rounds to the left of the decimal point: ROUND(156.786, -1) = 160.
  • TRUNC(n, d): cuts off the digits without rounding: 156.78.
  • CEIL(n): smallest integer ≥ n. FLOOR(n): largest integer ≤ n.
  • For negatives: ROUND(-2.5) = -3, while TRUNC(-2.7) = -2 (it just drops the decimals).

code.en:
SELECT ename, sal,
       ROUND(sal / 12, 2) monthly,
       MOD(sal, 7) m7,
       TRUNC(sal * 0.0833) bonus
FROM emp
WHERE deptno = 20;

expl.en:
• Functions are applied to every row of the result.
  • ROUND(sal / 12, 2) shows the monthly pay to 2 decimals. Oracle drops trailing zeros (5000, not 5000.00); use TO_CHAR to format.
  • MOD(sal, 7) gives the remainder when the salary is divided by 7.
  • TRUNC(sal * 0.0833): bonus with the paise removed.

code.en:
SELECT UPPER('gtu exam') u,
       LOWER('DIPLOMA') l,
       INITCAP('surat city') i,
       LENGTH('Gujarat') len
FROM dual;

SELECT ename, INITCAP(ename) name,
       LOWER(job) job,
       LENGTH(ename) len,
       CONCAT(ename, deptno) c,
       ename || '-' || job j
FROM emp
WHERE deptno = 10;

programs.out:
U        L       I          LEN
-------- ------- ---------- ---
GTU EXAM diploma Surat City   7

ENAME  NAME   JOB        LEN C        J
------ ------ ---------- --- -------- ----------------
RAJESH Rajesh president    6 RAJESH10 RAJESH-PRESIDENT
HETAL  Hetal  accountant   5 HETAL10  HETAL-ACCOUNTANT

expl.en:
• UPPER / LOWER: convert to capitals / small letters.
  • INITCAP: first letter of each word in capitals, the rest small.
  • LENGTH: number of characters.
  • CONCAT(a, b): joins exactly two strings (numbers are converted automatically). The || operator can join any number of strings.
  • Searching without worrying about case: WHERE UPPER(ename) = 'AMIT'.

title.en: Character functions: LTRIM, RTRIM, REPLACE, LPAD, RPAD

code.en:
SELECT LTRIM('   GTU') a,
       RTRIM('xxGTUxx', 'x') b,
       LTRIM('000123', '0') c,
       REPLACE('JACK AND JUE', 'J', 'BL') d
FROM dual;

SELECT LPAD(ename, 8, '*') lp,
       RPAD(ename, 8, '.') rp,
       LPAD(sal, 7, '0') sal
FROM emp
WHERE deptno = 10;

programs.out:
A   B     C   D
--- ----- --- --------------
GTU xxGTU 123 BLACK AND BLUE

LP       RP       SAL
-------- -------- -------
**RAJESH RAJESH.. 0090000
***HETAL HETAL... 0040000

expl.en:
• LTRIM(s, set) / RTRIM(s, set): remove the given characters (default: spaces) from the left / right end. TRIM(s) removes spaces from both ends.
  • LTRIM('000123', '0') removes leading zeros.
  • REPLACE(s, find, new): replaces every occurrence. Without the third argument the text is removed.
  • LPAD(s, n, c) / RPAD(s, n, c): pad on the left / right with character c up to total length n. LPAD is used to right-align numbers or add leading zeros.

code.en:
SELECT SUBSTR('GUJARAT', 3, 3) a,
       SUBSTR('GUJARAT', 4) b,
       SUBSTR('GUJARAT', -3) c,
       INSTR('GUJARAT', 'A') d,
       INSTR('GUJARAT', 'A', 1, 2) e,
       INSTR('GUJARAT', 'Z') f
FROM dual;

SELECT ename, SUBSTR(ename, 1, 3) code,
       INSTR(ename, 'A') pos_a
FROM emp
WHERE deptno = 30;

programs.out:
A   B    C   D E F
--- ---- --- - - -
JAR ARAT RAT 4 6 0

ENAME CODE POS_A
----- ---- -----
PRIYA PRI      5
SUNIL SUN      0
POOJA POO      5
VIJAY VIJ      4

expl.en:
• SUBSTR(s, start, len): extracts len characters from position start (the first character is 1). Without len it goes to the end. A negative start counts from the right.
  • INSTR(s, find, start, n): the position of the n-th occurrence of find, searching from start. It returns 0 if not found.
  • SUBSTR(ename, 1, 3) makes a 3-letter code; INSTR gives 0 for SUNIL because it has no A.

title.en: Date functions: SYSDATE, ADD_MONTHS, MONTHS_BETWEEN, NEXT_DAY, LAST_DAY

code.en:
SELECT SYSDATE today,
       ADD_MONTHS(SYSDATE, 3) plus3,
       ADD_MONTHS(SYSDATE, -1) minus1,
       LAST_DAY(SYSDATE) last,
       NEXT_DAY(SYSDATE, 'MONDAY') nxt
FROM dual;

SELECT ename, hiredate,
       ROUND(MONTHS_BETWEEN(SYSDATE,
             hiredate)) months,
       ADD_MONTHS(hiredate, 6) probation
FROM emp
WHERE deptno = 10;

expl.en:
• SYSDATE: the current date and time of the server.
  • ADD_MONTHS(d, n): adds n months (n may be negative). If d is the last day of a month, the result is the last day of the new month (31-JAN + 1 → 28/29-FEB).
  • MONTHS_BETWEEN(d1, d2): the number of months from d2 to d1 (it can be fractional); positive if d1 is later.
  • LAST_DAY(d): the last date of d's month.
  • NEXT_DAY(d, 'DAY'): the date of the next given weekday after d. 28-OCT-26 is a Wednesday, so the next Monday is 02-NOV-26.

title.en: ROUND and TRUNC on dates, and date arithmetic

code.en:
SELECT ROUND(SYSDATE, 'MONTH') rm,
       TRUNC(SYSDATE, 'MONTH') tm,
       ROUND(SYSDATE, 'YEAR') ry,
       TRUNC(SYSDATE, 'YEAR') ty
FROM dual;

SELECT ename,
       TRUNC(SYSDATE - hiredate) days,
       TRUNC((SYSDATE - hiredate) / 7)
         weeks,
       hiredate + 90 review
FROM emp
WHERE deptno = 10;

expl.en:
• ROUND(d, 'MONTH'): to the 1st of the nearest month (day 16 or later rounds up). 28-OCT → 01-NOV.
  • TRUNC(d, 'MONTH'): to the 1st of the same month. 'YEAR' works the same way (July or later rounds up to the next year).
  • Date arithmetic: date − date = number of days (with a fraction for the time); date + n = the date n days later.
  • TRUNC removes the fractional day, so we get complete days and weeks.

code.en:
SELECT TO_CHAR(SYSDATE, 'DD/MM/YYYY') a,
       TO_CHAR(SYSDATE, 'DD-MON-YYYY') b,
       TO_CHAR(SYSDATE, 'fmDay, DD Month')
         c,
       TO_CHAR(SYSDATE, 'HH24:MI:SS') t
FROM dual;

SELECT ename,
       TO_CHAR(hiredate, 'YYYY') yr,
       TO_CHAR(hiredate, 'Mon') mon,
       TO_CHAR(sal, '99,999.99') salary
FROM emp
WHERE deptno = 20;

expl.en:
TO_CHAR(date, 'format') converts a date to text in any format.

  • Elements: DD day, MM month number, MON JAN, MONTH JANUARY, YY/YYYY year, DAY weekday, DY WED, HH24:MI:SS time, Q quarter.
  • The case of the format controls the output: Mon → Mar, MON → MAR.
  • fm (fill mode) removes extra spaces from Day and Month names.
  • TO_CHAR(number, '99,999.99'): 9 = a digit, comma = thousands separator, period = decimal point. One extra leading space is kept for the sign.

code.en:
SELECT TO_DATE('15-08-2026',
               'DD-MM-YYYY') d1,
       TO_DATE('January 26, 2027',
               'Month DD, YYYY') d2
FROM dual;

SELECT TO_NUMBER('5,000', '9,999') + 1 n,
       TO_NUMBER('12.75') * 2 m
FROM dual;

SELECT ename, hiredate FROM emp
WHERE hiredate > TO_DATE('01-01-2021',
                         'DD-MM-YYYY');

expl.en:
• TO_DATE(text, 'format') converts text to a DATE. The format must describe the text exactly; the result is shown in the default DD-MON-YY format.
  • TO_NUMBER(text, 'format') converts text (which may contain commas) to a number so arithmetic can be done.
  • Always compare dates using TO_DATE, never with a plain string, because the default date format can differ between systems.

code.en:
SELECT ename, comm,
       NVL(comm, 0) c,
       sal + NVL(comm, 0) total,
       NVL2(comm, 'YES', 'NO') has_comm
FROM emp
WHERE deptno = 30;

SELECT ename, deptno,
       DECODE(deptno, 10, 'ACCOUNTS',
                      20, 'RESEARCH',
                      30, 'SALES',
                      'NO DEPT') dept
FROM emp
WHERE empno IN (101, 102, 103, 110);

programs.out:
ENAME COMM    C TOTAL HAS_COMM
----- ---- ---- ----- --------
PRIYA         0 58000 NO
SUNIL 3000 3000 33000 YES
POOJA 5000 5000 33000 YES
VIJAY         0 20000 NO

ENAME  DEPTNO DEPT
------ ------ --------
RAJESH     10 ACCOUNTS
AMIT       20 RESEARCH
PRIYA      30 SALES
MEHUL         NO DEPT

expl.en:
• NVL(expr, value): if expr is NULL, return value; otherwise return expr. Used to treat a missing commission as 0.
  • NVL2(expr, a, b): returns a if expr is not NULL, otherwise b.
  • DECODE(expr, s1, r1, s2, r2, ..., default): works like an IF-THEN-ELSE / switch-case. It compares expr with each search value and returns the matching result, or the default. MEHUL has no department, so he gets 'NO DEPT'.
  • The standard SQL equivalent of DECODE is the CASE expression.

code.en:
SELECT COUNT(*) emps, COUNT(comm) c,
       SUM(sal) total, MAX(sal) max,
       MIN(sal) min, AVG(sal) avg
FROM emp;

SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT job) jobs,
       MIN(hiredate) first,
       MAX(ename) last_name
FROM emp;

expl.en:
• Aggregate (group) functions return one result for a set of rows.
  • COUNT(*) counts all rows; COUNT(comm) counts only non-NULL values (2). All aggregates except COUNT(*) ignore NULLs.
  • SUM and AVG work on numbers; MAX, MIN and COUNT also work on dates and text (MAX(ename) = alphabetically last).
  • COUNT(DISTINCT job) counts the different jobs.

code.en:
SELECT deptno, COUNT(*) emps,
       SUM(sal) total,
       ROUND(AVG(sal)) avg
FROM emp
WHERE deptno IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY deptno
ORDER BY deptno;

SELECT deptno, job, COUNT(*) n
FROM emp
WHERE deptno IN (20, 30)
GROUP BY deptno, job
ORDER BY deptno, n DESC, job;

programs.out:
DEPTNO EMPS  TOTAL   AVG
------ ---- ------ -----
    10    2 130000 65000
    20    3 127000 42333
    30    4 136000 34000

DEPTNO JOB      N
------ -------- -
    20 ANALYST  1
    20 CLERK    1
    20 MANAGER  1
    30 SALESMAN 2
    30 CLERK    1
    30 MANAGER  1

6 rows selected.

expl.en:
• GROUP BY divides the rows into groups with the same value(s); each aggregate is calculated per group, giving one row per group.
  • Every column in the SELECT list that is not inside an aggregate function must be in GROUP BY (otherwise: ORA-00979 not a GROUP BY expression).
  • Grouping by two columns makes one group for every (deptno, job) combination.
  • ORDER BY sorts the final result; DESC gives descending order, and the alias n can be used. Without ORDER BY, Oracle does not guarantee any row order.

code.en:
SELECT deptno, COUNT(*) emps,
       AVG(sal) avg_sal
FROM emp
WHERE deptno IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY deptno
HAVING COUNT(*) > 2;

SELECT job, SUM(sal) total
FROM emp
WHERE job <> 'PRESIDENT'
GROUP BY job
HAVING SUM(sal) >= 50000
ORDER BY total DESC;

expl.en:
• WHERE filters rows before grouping; it cannot use aggregate functions.
  • HAVING filters groups after grouping; it is used with aggregate functions.
  • Second query: the president row is removed first (WHERE), then the rows are grouped by job, and only jobs with a total salary of at least 50000 are kept (HAVING). The result is sorted by total.

title.en: ORDER BY: ascending, descending, multiple columns, NULLs

code.en:
SELECT ename, deptno, sal
FROM emp
WHERE sal >= 40000
ORDER BY deptno, sal DESC;

SELECT ename, comm FROM emp
WHERE deptno = 30
ORDER BY comm DESC;

SELECT ename, sal * 12 annual
FROM emp
WHERE deptno = 20
ORDER BY 2;

programs.out:
ENAME  DEPTNO   SAL
------ ------ -----
RAJESH     10 90000
HETAL      10 40000
AMIT       20 60000
NEHA       20 45000
PRIYA      30 58000

ENAME COMM
----- ----
PRIYA
VIJAY
POOJA 5000
SUNIL 3000

ENAME ANNUAL
----- ------
KIRAN 264000
NEHA  540000
AMIT  720000

expl.en:
• ORDER BY deptno, sal DESC: sort by deptno (ascending, the default); within the same deptno, by salary in descending order.
  • In Oracle, NULLs are treated as the largest value: they come last in ASC and first in DESC (change with NULLS FIRST / NULLS LAST).
  • You can sort by a column position (ORDER BY 2) or by an alias.
  • ORDER BY is always the last clause of a query.

code.en:
SELECT e.ename, e.job, d.dname, d.loc
FROM emp e INNER JOIN dept d
ON e.deptno = d.deptno
WHERE e.sal >= 45000;

-- Oracle traditional syntax
SELECT e.ename, d.dname
FROM emp e, dept d
WHERE e.deptno = d.deptno
AND d.loc = 'VADODARA';

-- Non-equi join
SELECT e.ename, e.sal, s.grade
FROM emp e JOIN salgrade s
ON e.sal BETWEEN s.losal AND s.hisal
WHERE e.deptno = 30
ORDER BY s.grade, e.ename;

programs.out:
ENAME  JOB       DNAME    LOC
------ --------- -------- ---------
RAJESH PRESIDENT ACCOUNTS SURAT
AMIT   MANAGER   RESEARCH AHMEDABAD
PRIYA  MANAGER   SALES    VADODARA
NEHA   ANALYST   RESEARCH AHMEDABAD

ENAME DNAME
----- -----
PRIYA SALES
SUNIL SALES
POOJA SALES
VIJAY SALES

ENAME   SAL GRADE
----- ----- -----
POOJA 28000     2
VIJAY 20000     2
SUNIL 30000     3
PRIYA 58000     4

expl.en:
• An inner join returns only the rows that have a match in both tables. MEHUL (no department) and OPERATIONS (no employees) never appear.
  • An equi join uses = in the join condition. The ANSI syntax uses JOIN ... ON; the traditional Oracle syntax lists the tables with commas and puts the condition in WHERE.
  • Table aliases (e, d) make the query short, and they are needed when both tables have a column with the same name (deptno).
  • A non-equi join uses an operator other than = (here BETWEEN) to match each salary with its grade.

title.en: Outer joins: LEFT, RIGHT and FULL

code.en:
SELECT e.ename, d.dname
FROM emp e LEFT OUTER JOIN dept d
ON e.deptno = d.deptno
WHERE e.empno >= 108;

SELECT d.dname, COUNT(e.empno) emps
FROM emp e RIGHT OUTER JOIN dept d
ON e.deptno = d.deptno
GROUP BY d.dname
ORDER BY emps;

SELECT e.ename, d.dname
FROM emp e FULL OUTER JOIN dept d
ON e.deptno = d.deptno
WHERE e.ename IS NULL
   OR d.dname IS NULL;

programs.out:
ENAME DNAME
----- --------
VIJAY SALES
HETAL ACCOUNTS
MEHUL

DNAME      EMPS
---------- ----
OPERATIONS    0
ACCOUNTS      2
RESEARCH      3
SALES         4

ENAME DNAME
----- ----------
MEHUL
      OPERATIONS

expl.en:
• LEFT OUTER JOIN: all rows of the left table (emp) plus the matching rows of the right table. MEHUL appears with a NULL dname.
  • RIGHT OUTER JOIN: all rows of the right table (dept). OPERATIONS appears with no employee, so COUNT(e.empno) = 0.
  • FULL OUTER JOIN: all rows of both tables. The WHERE keeps only the unmatched rows from either side.
  • Old Oracle syntax for an outer join uses (+) on the side that may be missing: WHERE e.deptno = d.deptno(+) is a left join.

code.en:
SELECT e.ename, d.dname
FROM emp e CROSS JOIN dept d
WHERE e.empno = 101;

SELECT w.ename worker, m.ename manager
FROM emp w JOIN emp m
ON w.mgr = m.empno
WHERE m.job = 'MANAGER'
ORDER BY manager, worker;

programs.out:
ENAME  DNAME
------ ----------
RAJESH ACCOUNTS
RAJESH RESEARCH
RAJESH SALES
RAJESH OPERATIONS

WORKER MANAGER
------ -------
KIRAN  AMIT
NEHA   AMIT
POOJA  PRIYA
SUNIL  PRIYA
VIJAY  PRIYA

expl.en:
• A cross join (Cartesian product) pairs every row of one table with every row of the other: 10 × 4 = 40 rows. Here only RAJESH's 4 combinations are shown.
  • A self join joins a table with itself using two different aliases. Here w plays the worker and m plays the manager; the condition w.mgr = m.empno finds each worker's manager.
  • Use LEFT JOIN in the self join to also list RAJESH, who has no manager.

programs.out:
ENAME    SAL
------ -----
RAJESH 90000
AMIT   60000
PRIYA  58000
NEHA   45000

ENAME JOB
----- -------
NEHA  ANALYST

ENAME  DEPTNO
------ ------
RAJESH     10
HETAL      10

expl.en:
• A sub-query (inner query) is a SELECT inside another SQL statement. The inner query runs first and its result is used by the outer query.
  • Single-row sub-query: returns one value. Use single-row operators = > < >= <= <>. The average salary is 40800.
  • Multiple-row sub-query: returns many values. Use IN, ANY, ALL or EXISTS. Using = with many rows gives ORA-01427.
  • A sub-query is always written in brackets and cannot have its own ORDER BY.

code.en:
-- Employees working in the department
-- of the highest-paid manager
SELECT ename, job, deptno FROM emp
WHERE deptno =
  (SELECT deptno FROM emp
   WHERE sal =
     (SELECT MAX(sal) FROM emp
      WHERE job = 'MANAGER'));

-- 2nd highest salary
SELECT MAX(sal) second_max FROM emp
WHERE sal < (SELECT MAX(sal) FROM emp);

programs.out:
ENAME JOB     DEPTNO
----- ------- ------
AMIT  MANAGER     20
NEHA  ANALYST     20
KIRAN CLERK       20

SECOND_MAX
----------
     60000

expl.en:
Sub-queries can be nested inside each other (up to 255 levels in Oracle). The innermost query runs first:

  1. Level 3: MAX(sal) of managers = 60000.
  2. Level 2: the deptno of the employee earning 60000 = 20.
  3. Level 1: all employees of department 20.

The second query is a classic exam question: the highest salary among those that are less than the overall maximum gives the 2nd highest salary.

code.en:
-- Earns more than own dept average
SELECT e.ename, e.deptno, e.sal
FROM emp e
WHERE e.sal > (SELECT AVG(sal)
               FROM emp
               WHERE deptno = e.deptno);

-- Highest paid in each department
SELECT ename, deptno, sal FROM emp e
WHERE sal = (SELECT MAX(sal) FROM emp
             WHERE deptno = e.deptno)
ORDER BY deptno;

programs.out:
ENAME  DEPTNO   SAL
------ ------ -----
RAJESH     10 90000
AMIT       20 60000
PRIYA      30 58000
NEHA       20 45000

ENAME  DEPTNO   SAL
------ ------ -----
RAJESH     10 90000
AMIT       20 60000
PRIYA      30 58000

expl.en:
• In a correlated sub-query, the inner query uses a column of the outer query (e.deptno), so it cannot run alone.
  • It is executed once for every row of the outer query: for NEHA (dept 20), it calculates the average of dept 20 (42333.33) and compares her salary 45000.
  • A normal (nested) sub-query runs only once; a correlated sub-query runs many times, so it can be slower.
  • MEHUL has a NULL deptno, so deptno = NULL never matches and he is not listed.

title.en: Set operators: UNION, UNION ALL, INTERSECT, MINUS

programs.out:
JOB
----------
ACCOUNTANT
CLERK
MANAGER
PRESIDENT
SALESMAN

JOB
----------
PRESIDENT
ACCOUNTANT
MANAGER
SALESMAN
SALESMAN
CLERK

6 rows selected.

JOB
-------
CLERK
MANAGER

DEPTNO
------
    40

expl.en:
• UNION: rows from both queries, with duplicates removed and the result sorted.
  • UNION ALL: all rows from both queries, including duplicates (SALESMAN twice), not sorted. It is faster.
  • INTERSECT: only rows present in both results: jobs found in both dept 20 and 30.
  • MINUS: rows of the first query that are not in the second: departments without employees (40).
  • Both queries must select the same number of columns with compatible types.

title.en: Order of Execution of a SELECT

items.f:
WHERE col IN (v1, v2, ...)
WHERE col BETWEEN low AND high
WHERE col LIKE 'pattern'
WHERE col IS NULL
WHERE col > ANY (sub-query)
WHERE col > ALL (sub-query)
WHERE EXISTS (sub-query)

terms.en: BETWEEN includes both limits. Use IS NULL, never = NULL.

items.f:
'A%'   starts with A
'%A'   ends with A
'_A%'  2nd letter A
'___'  exactly 3 chars

terms.en: % = zero or more characters, _ = exactly one character.

items.f:
ABS(n)  POWER(m,n)  MOD(m,n)
SQRT(n)  CEIL(n)  FLOOR(n)
ROUND(n[,d])  TRUNC(n[,d])

LOWER(s) UPPER(s) INITCAP(s)
LENGTH(s) CONCAT(a,b) a || b
LTRIM(s[,set]) RTRIM(s[,set])
REPLACE(s,find[,new])
SUBSTR(s,start[,len])
INSTR(s,find[,start[,n]])
LPAD(s,n[,c]) RPAD(s,n[,c])

terms.en: Positions start at 1. INSTR returns 0 if not found.

items.f:
SYSDATE
ADD_MONTHS(d, n)
MONTHS_BETWEEN(d1, d2)
LAST_DAY(d)
NEXT_DAY(d, 'DAY')
ROUND(d[, 'MONTH'|'YEAR'])
TRUNC(d[, 'MONTH'|'YEAR'])

terms.en: date ± n = date; date − date = days.
Format elements: DD MM MON MONTH YY YYYY DAY DY HH24 MI SS; 9 0 , . $

items.f:
NVL(e, v)
NVL2(e, if_not_null, if_null)
DECODE(e, s1, r1, s2, r2, def)

terms.en: DECODE works like IF-THEN-ELSE for equality tests.

items.f:
SELECT ename, sal,
  CASE
    WHEN sal >= 50000 THEN 'HIGH'
    WHEN sal >= 25000 THEN 'MEDIUM'
    ELSE 'LOW'
  END AS category
FROM emp
WHERE deptno = 30;

terms.en: ANSI standard; can test any condition.

items.f:
SELECT col, aggregate(col2)
FROM table
[WHERE row_condition]
GROUP BY col
[HAVING group_condition]
[ORDER BY col [ASC | DESC]];

terms.en: WHERE filters rows; HAVING filters groups.

items.f:
ORDER BY col1 [ASC | DESC]
        [NULLS FIRST | NULLS LAST],
         col2 [ASC | DESC], ...

terms.en: Default ASC. Can use alias or column position.

items.f:
COUNT(*)  COUNT(col)
COUNT(DISTINCT col)
SUM(col)  AVG(col)
MAX(col)  MIN(col)

SELECT t1.col, t2.col
FROM t1 [INNER] JOIN t2
ON t1.key = t2.key;

-- Oracle traditional syntax
SELECT t1.col, t2.col
FROM t1, t2
WHERE t1.key = t2.key;

terms.en: Joins on columns with the same name.

items.f:
FROM t1 LEFT  [OUTER] JOIN t2 ON ...
FROM t1 RIGHT [OUTER] JOIN t2 ON ...
FROM t1 FULL  [OUTER] JOIN t2 ON ...

-- Oracle (+) syntax: + on the side
-- that may have no matching row
WHERE e.deptno = d.deptno(+)  -- LEFT
WHERE e.deptno(+) = d.deptno  -- RIGHT

terms.en: (+) goes on the side that may be missing.

items.f:
SELECT columns FROM table
WHERE col operator
      (SELECT col FROM table
       WHERE condition);

terms.en: Single-row: = > <. Multiple-row: IN ANY ALL EXISTS.

items.f:
-- in UPDATE
UPDATE emp SET sal = sal * 1.1
WHERE deptno = (SELECT deptno FROM dept
                WHERE dname = 'SALES');

-- in FROM (inline view)
SELECT d, avg_sal
FROM (SELECT deptno d, AVG(sal) avg_sal
      FROM emp GROUP BY deptno)
WHERE avg_sal > 40000;

terms.en: A sub-query in FROM is called an inline view.

items.f:
SELECT col_list FROM t1
UNION | UNION ALL | INTERSECT | MINUS
SELECT col_list FROM t2
[ORDER BY ...];

terms.en: Same number and type of columns; ORDER BY only at the end.

q.en: What are the special operators in SQL?

a.en: IN, BETWEEN, LIKE, IS NULL, ANY, ALL and EXISTS (and their NOT forms).

q.en: What is the difference between % and _ in LIKE?

a.en: % matches zero or more characters; _ matches exactly one character.

q.en: Does BETWEEN include the boundary values?

a.en: Yes. BETWEEN 10 AND 20 includes 10 and 20.

q.en: Why can't we write comm = NULL?

a.en: NULL means unknown, so a comparison with it is never true. Use IS NULL.

q.en: What is the result of 5000 + NULL?

a.en: NULL. Any arithmetic with NULL gives NULL; use NVL to avoid it.

q.en: What is the DUAL table?

a.en: A one-row, one-column dummy table owned by SYS, used to evaluate expressions and functions.

q.en: Difference between ROUND and TRUNC?

a.en: ROUND rounds to the nearest value; TRUNC simply cuts off the digits. ROUND(4.56,1) = 4.6, TRUNC(4.56,1) = 4.5.

q.en: Difference between CEIL and FLOOR?

a.en: CEIL returns the smallest integer ≥ n; FLOOR returns the largest integer ≤ n.

q.en: What does MOD(17, 5) return?

a.en: 2, the remainder of 17 divided by 5.

q.en: What does INITCAP do?

a.en: It converts the first letter of every word to capital and the rest to small letters.

q.en: What is the difference between SUBSTR and INSTR?

a.en: SUBSTR extracts part of a string; INSTR returns the position of a substring.

q.en: What is the difference between CONCAT and ||?

a.en: CONCAT joins exactly two strings; || can join any number of strings.

q.en: What does LPAD('5', 3, '0') return?
What does LAST_DAY return?

a.en: The date of the last day of the month of the given date.

q.en: What does NEXT_DAY(SYSDATE, 'FRIDAY') return?

a.en: The date of the first Friday after today.

q.en: What is the result of subtracting two dates?

a.en: The number of days between them.

q.en: Name the conversion functions.

a.en: TO_CHAR, TO_DATE and TO_NUMBER.

q.en: What is the use of NVL?

a.en: It replaces NULL with a given value, e.g. NVL(comm, 0).

q.en: What is DECODE?

a.en: Oracle's IF-THEN-ELSE function that compares an expression with search values and returns the matching result.

q.en: Name the aggregate functions.

a.en: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX and MIN.

q.en: Difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(column)?

a.en: COUNT(*) counts all rows; COUNT(column) counts only non-NULL values of that column.

q.en: Difference between WHERE and HAVING?

a.en: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after grouping and can use aggregate functions.

q.en: What is the default order of ORDER BY?

a.en: Ascending (ASC).

q.en: Where do NULLs appear in ORDER BY ASC in Oracle?

a.en: Last (NULLs are treated as the largest values).

q.en: What is a join?

a.en: An operation that combines rows of two or more tables based on a related column.

q.en: What is an equi join?

a.en: A join that uses the = operator in the join condition.

q.en: What is a non-equi join?

a.en: A join that uses an operator other than =, such as BETWEEN or >.

q.en: What is an outer join?

a.en: A join that returns matching rows plus the non-matching rows of one or both tables, with NULLs for the missing columns.

q.en: What is a self join?

a.en: A join of a table with itself using two aliases, e.g. to find each employee's manager.

q.en: How many rows does a cross join of 5 and 4 rows give?
What is a sub-query?

a.en: A query written inside another SQL statement; its result is used by the outer query.

q.en: What is a correlated sub-query?

a.en: A sub-query that uses a column of the outer query and is executed once for each outer row.

q.en: What error occurs when a single-row sub-query returns many rows?

a.en: ORA-01427: single-row subquery returns more than one row.

q.en: Difference between UNION and UNION ALL?

a.en: UNION removes duplicates and sorts; UNION ALL keeps all rows, including duplicates.

q.en: What does MINUS return?

a.en: The rows of the first query that are not returned by the second query.

q.en: What are the rules for set operators?

a.en: Same number of columns, compatible data types; ORDER BY only at the end.
